title: Factory's two independent choices
description: Separate configuration storage from the engine that runs Agents.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional team choosing Factory settings. They see configuration storage and engine options. Are those two names for the same decision?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Storage decides where Factory keeps configuration and how it reaches Agents. The engine decides how Agents run. Keeping the two questions separate prevents a storage choice from being mistaken for a new runtime.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the practical difference between the storage choices?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: JSON uses local files. ConfigMaps and Secrets deliver environment configuration through Kubernetes, without requiring MongoDB. The MongoDB option retains the database-backed behaviour. Sensitive settings need appropriate protection; base64 encoding alone is not encryption.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Could our team select the listed Docker engine and avoid Kubernetes today?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not according to this guide. Kubernetes is the implemented engine. Docker and host engines are planned. Configuration support being engine-independent does not mean those runtimes already exist.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How should an existing installation approach the new settings?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use the explicit configuration and engine settings for new deployments, and review the documented legacy fallback for older ones. Agents can also opt into Kubernetes-backed configuration gradually. Choose a supported combination and test it before changing the whole fleet.
